case.case_title: Peter Leo Fernando v. The Attorney-General and Two Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 31/85, decided on 11 July 1985

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the detention of the petitioner by the Magistrate without proper procedure violated the petitioner's fundamental right to freedom of movement and residence under Article 14(1)(h) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that his fundamental rights under Articles 11, 13(1), 13(2), and 14(1)(h) were infringed by his unlawful detention and sought relief and damages.
case_context.respondent_argument: The 2nd respondent (Magistrate) argued that the detention was a judicial act done in good faith within his jurisdiction and thus immune from liability. The detention did not constitute executive or administrative action under Articles 17 and 126 of the Constitution.
key_facts: Petitioner was detained in the Magistrate's Court cell for about four hours on the Magistrate's order without proper procedure under the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The complaint used to justify detention did not mention the petitioner threatening to shoot anyone.
The Magistrate did not examine the complainant on oath before ordering detention as required by law.
The petitioner was not a party or witness in the case being heard.
The petitioner was released after the complaint was verified and found baseless.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that judicial acts, even if unlawful or mistaken, are immune from claims under Articles 17 and 126 which apply only to executive or administrative action. The Magistrate's detention order was a judicial act done in good faith and thus not actionable under fundamental rights provisions for executive or administrative action.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Magistrate's order, though procedurally flawed, was a judicial act within his jurisdiction and done in good faith. The detention was not executive or administrative action but a judicial act, so the petitioner was not entitled to relief under Articles 17 and 126 for violation of freedom of movement.
principles_established: Judges have immunity from civil liability for acts done in the exercise of judicial functions done in good faith.
Unlawful judicial orders do not convert judicial acts into executive or administrative acts.
Relief under Articles 17 and 126 is available only against executive or administrative action, not judicial action.
The remedy for judicial errors is by appeal, not by fundamental rights application under Articles 17 and 126.
State liability for judicial acts is limited and does not extend to judges personally.
precedents_cited: Sirros v. Moore and Others [1974] 3 All ER 776
Maharaj v. Attorney-General of Trinidad and Tobago (No. 2) [1979] AC 385
A. K. Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Others
Wijetunga v. Insurance Corporation and Another
Naresh S. Murajikar v. State of Maharashtra
Chokalinge v. Attorney-General of Trinidad and Tobago
Dayananda v. Weeratunga Si. Police et al.

outcome.holding: The application for relief under Articles 17 and 126 was dismissed as the detention was a judicial act and not executive or administrative action. The petitioner was not entitled to relief for alleged violation of freedom of movement under Article 14(1)(h).

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: The petitioner's claim included violation of freedom of movement under Article 14(1)(h) due to unlawful detention. The Court's reasoning centered on whether the detention constituted executive or administrative action under Articles 17 and 126, which is necessary for relief under fundamental rights including Article 14(1)(h).

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner was detained in the court cell for about four hours on the Magistrate's order without proper procedure under the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court held that such detention was a judicial act done in good faith and not executive or administrative action under Articles 17 and 126.
